people.name: Pelé
people.why: The only player to win three World Cups, and for decades the most famous person on earth.

people.name: Tom Jobim
people.why: Co-wrote 'The Girl from Ipanema' and effectively invented bossa nova.

people.name: Oscar Niemeyer
people.why: Designed Brasília's curving white monuments and kept working past his hundredth birthday.

people.name: Machado de Assis
people.why: A mixed-race grandson of freed slaves who became Brazil's greatest writer, and its most quietly savage ironist.

people.name: Ayrton Senna
people.why: Three-time Formula One champion whose death in 1994 brought Brazil to a standstill.

events.title: Cabral lands in Bahia
events.what: Portugal claimed the coast, beginning three centuries of colonial rule built on sugar and enslaved labour.

events.title: Independence
events.what: The Portuguese king's own son declared Brazil independent and crowned himself emperor — a monarchy in the Americas that lasted until 1889.

events.title: The Golden Law
events.what: Brazil abolished slavery — the last country in the Americas to do so, after importing more enslaved Africans than anywhere else.

events.title: Brasília opens
events.what: A capital built from nothing in 41 months, in the empty centre of the country, to pull development inland.

events.title: Return to democracy
events.what: Twenty-one years of military dictatorship ended; the 1988 constitution is still called the Citizen's Constitution.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Feijoada — black beans slow-cooked with pork — is the Saturday lunch that takes the whole afternoon.

culture.label: Festival
culture.text: Carnival is a national shutdown. Rio's samba schools compete in a purpose-built stadium; Salvador's street party is bigger still.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Football is close to a national religion. Ask someone their club before you ask their politics.

culture.label: Greeting
culture.text: Personal space is small and warmth is immediate. Hugs, cheek kisses and touching your arm mid-sentence are all normal.

culture.label: Music
culture.text: Samba, bossa nova, forró, funk carioca and sertanejo all coexist; regional identity runs through what people listen to.

talkAbout: Which regional cuisine they think is best — the north-east and the south will give you very different answers.
Their football club, and how the season is going.
Music: almost everyone has strong opinions about sertanejo versus everything else.
avoid: Don't assume Brazil is 'Latin American like the rest' — Brazilians speak Portuguese, not Spanish, and the distinction matters. Racial inequality and the Amazon are discussed openly but are not light small talk.

people.name: Jorge Luis Borges
people.why: His labyrinth stories reshaped world literature; he ran the national library after going blind.

people.name: Eva Perón
people.why: Rose from rural poverty to become the most adored and most hated woman in Argentine history.

people.name: Diego Maradona
people.why: Won the 1986 World Cup almost single-handedly, and is mourned as a folk saint.

people.name: Lionel Messi
people.why: Eight Ballons d'Or, and the 2022 World Cup that finally settled the argument.

people.name: Pope Francis
people.why: The first Latin American pope, and a Buenos Aires priest to the end.

events.title: Independence declared
events.what: The United Provinces broke from Spain at Tucumán, six years into a war led by José de San Martín.

events.title: The great immigration
events.what: Millions of Italians and Spaniards arrived; by 1914 a third of the country was foreign-born, which is why Argentine Spanish sounds Italian.

events.title: Perón elected
events.what: Peronism reshaped Argentine politics around the unions and the poor, and still defines the country's political fault line.

events.title: The Dirty War
events.what: A military junta disappeared an estimated 30,000 people; the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo still march every Thursday.

events.title: The economic collapse
events.what: Default, frozen bank accounts and five presidents in two weeks — the reference point for every crisis since.

culture.label: Mate
culture.text: A shared gourd of bitter tea passed around a group. Being offered it is an invitation; refusing outright is odd.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: The asado is a slow weekend barbecue run by one designated griller, and it is a social institution, not a meal.

culture.label: Dance
culture.text: Tango was born in the port slums of Buenos Aires and is danced seriously in milongas to this day.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: The Boca–River rivalry is one of the fiercest in world sport.

culture.label: Timing
culture.text: Dinner starts at ten, and an invitation for nine means arriving at half past.

talkAbout: Football — but ask which club, not whether they follow it.
Whether Argentine beef really is better, and why they think so.
Buenos Aires versus the provinces; everyone has a view on the capital.
avoid: The Falklands/Malvinas are a national wound, not a debating point. The 1976–83 dictatorship is discussed but carefully — most families were touched by it.

people.name: Gabriel García Márquez
people.why: One Hundred Years of Solitude made magical realism the world's shorthand for Latin American writing; Nobel Prize, 1982.

people.name: Shakira
people.why: The best-selling Latin artist of all time, from Barranquilla on the Caribbean coast.

people.name: Fernando Botero
people.why: His inflated, rounded figures are instantly recognisable and fill public squares in Medellín.

people.name: Simón Bolívar
people.why: Venezuelan-born, but Colombia was the heart of his Gran Colombia; he died near Santa Marta.

people.name: Juan Manuel Santos
people.why: Won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016 for the deal that ended a fifty-year war with the FARC.

events.title: Battle of Boyacá
events.what: Bolívar's victory sealed independence from Spain and created Gran Colombia.

events.title: El Bogotazo
events.what: The assassination of Jorge Eliécer Gaitán set off riots and a decade of civil war known simply as La Violencia.

events.title: Escobar killed
events.what: The end of the Medellín cartel's most violent chapter, though not of the drug war.

events.title: The FARC peace accord
events.what: Ended the longest-running armed conflict in the Americas, narrowly rejected in a referendum and then revised and signed.

culture.label: Coffee
culture.text: The coffee-growing landscape is UNESCO-listed. A tinto is a small black coffee offered all day, everywhere.

culture.label: Music
culture.text: Cumbia and vallenato are the roots; salsa belongs to Cali, which claims to be its world capital.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Bandeja paisa is an enormous plate of beans, rice, pork, egg and plantain. Arepas are eaten everywhere, differently in every region.

culture.label: Festival
culture.text: Medellín's Feria de las Flores fills the city with flower displays carried on growers' backs.

culture.label: Manner
culture.text: Formality and warmth together — usted is common even among friends, alongside a lot of affection.

talkAbout: Regional identity: paisa, costeño, rolo and caleño are real and strongly felt distinctions.
Coffee, and why they think Colombian coffee is different.
How much the country has changed in the last twenty years — most people are keen to say so.
avoid: Drug-cartel jokes and Escobar references land badly; that era killed a great many ordinary people and Colombians are tired of being defined by it.

people.name: Mario Vargas Llosa
people.why: Nobel laureate in 2010, and once a presidential candidate.

people.name: Túpac Amaru II
people.why: Led the largest indigenous uprising against Spanish rule; his execution became a founding story of Andean resistance.

people.name: Gastón Acurio
people.why: Turned Peruvian cooking into a global cuisine and a source of national pride.

people.name: César Vallejo
people.why: The most radical Spanish-language poet of the twentieth century, who died poor in Paris.

people.name: Pachacuti
people.why: Turned a small kingdom into the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas, and probably built Machu Picchu.

events.title: The Inca Empire
events.what: Ruled 12 million people from Cusco across the Andes, with roads and record-keeping but no writing or wheel.

events.title: Pizarro at Cajamarca
events.what: 168 Spaniards captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa and brought down the empire within a year.

events.title: Machu Picchu revealed
events.what: Hiram Bingham brought the Inca citadel to world attention; local farmers had known it was there all along.

events.title: The Shining Path conflict
events.what: A Maoist insurgency and the state's response killed nearly 70,000 people, most of them rural and Quechua-speaking.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Ceviche — raw fish cured in lime — is eaten at lunchtime, never dinner. Peru has around 4,000 varieties of potato.

culture.label: Geography
culture.text: Coast, Andes and Amazon are three different countries in one, and people identify strongly with theirs.

culture.label: Textiles
culture.text: Andean weaving encodes community and status in its patterns, and is still worn rather than performed.

culture.label: Drink
culture.text: Pisco sour is the national cocktail, and its origin is a genuine and unresolved argument with Chile.

culture.label: Language
culture.text: Quechua and Aymara are official alongside Spanish, and millions speak them at home.

talkAbout: Food — Peruvians will happily talk about it for an hour, and Lima's restaurants are a point of pride.
Whether Machu Picchu or Choquequirao is the better ruin.
The three regions, and which one they are from.
avoid: Don't tell a Peruvian that pisco is Chilean. The Shining Path years and the Fujimori era remain politically raw.

people.name: Pablo Neruda
people.why: Nobel laureate whose love poems are recited across the Spanish-speaking world; also a diplomat and senator.

people.name: Gabriela Mistral
people.why: The first Latin American writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1945.

people.name: Violeta Parra
people.why: Collected Chile's folk music and wrote 'Gracias a la Vida', one of the most covered songs in Spanish.

people.name: Salvador Allende
people.why: The world's first freely elected Marxist head of state; died in the 1973 coup.

people.name: Isabel Allende
people.why: The most widely read Spanish-language woman novelist alive.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Bernardo O'Higgins and San Martín's army secured Chile's break from Spain at Maipú.

events.title: War of the Pacific
events.what: Chile took the nitrate coast from Peru and Bolivia, leaving Bolivia landlocked — still a live grievance.

events.title: The coup
events.what: Pinochet's forces bombed the presidential palace on 11 September; seventeen years of dictatorship followed.

events.title: The 33 miners
events.what: Trapped 700 m down for 69 days and brought up alive, watched live by about a billion people.

culture.label: Wine
culture.text: Carmenère was thought extinct until it was found growing in Chile, mislabelled as merlot.

culture.label: Geography
culture.text: 4,300 km long and rarely 200 km wide, from the driest desert on earth to Patagonian ice.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Empanadas de pino at Independence Day, completos (loaded hot dogs) the rest of the year.

culture.label: Dance
culture.text: The cueca, danced with a handkerchief, is the national dance and compulsory at every September fiesta.

culture.label: Speech
culture.text: Chilean Spanish is famously fast and full of local slang — even other Spanish speakers struggle.

talkAbout: Wine, and which valley they rate.
Poetry — Neruda and Mistral are genuinely popular, not just school reading.
The landscape, and which end of the country they prefer.
avoid: The Pinochet years still split families; 11 September means 1973 here. The Mapuche land conflict in the south is contested and heated.

people.name: Simón Bolívar
people.why: Born in Caracas, he freed six countries from Spanish rule and is invoked by every side of Venezuelan politics.

people.name: Teresa Carreño
people.why: A child prodigy who played for Lincoln at the White House and toured the world for fifty years.

people.name: Gustavo Dudamel
people.why: Product of El Sistema, the free youth-orchestra programme, and now one of the world's leading conductors.

people.name: Rómulo Gallegos
people.why: Wrote Doña Bárbara, the great novel of the Venezuelan plains, and briefly led the country.

people.name: Hugo Chávez
people.why: Reshaped Venezuela and much of Latin American politics for a generation; still fiercely argued over.

events.title: Independence declared
events.what: The first Spanish American colony to declare independence outright, though the war ran another decade.

events.title: Oil at Barroso
events.what: A gusher near Lake Maracaibo turned an agricultural country into an oil state within a decade.

events.title: The Caracazo
events.what: Riots against austerity were put down with hundreds, perhaps thousands, of deaths — the beginning of the old order's collapse.

events.title: The exodus
events.what: Economic collapse has driven more than seven million people out of the country, the largest displacement in the Americas.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Arepas at any hour, and hallacas — banana-leaf parcels made by the whole family — at Christmas.

culture.label: Music
culture.text: El Sistema has put instruments in the hands of hundreds of thousands of children since 1975.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Baseball, not football, is the national game, and Venezuelan players fill Major League rosters.

culture.label: Landscape
culture.text: Angel Falls drops nearly a kilometre off a flat-topped tepui in the Gran Sabana.

culture.label: Manner
culture.text: Loud, funny and quick to include a stranger; humour under pressure is a point of pride.

talkAbout: Baseball, and which Venezuelan players they follow.
Food, especially arepas and how the fillings differ from Colombian ones.
Music, from El Sistema to gaita at Christmas.
avoid: Venezuelan politics divides families and much of the diaspora. Let them raise it, and don't assume which side they are on.

people.name: Oswaldo Guayasamín
people.why: His anguished portraits of Latin America's poor are the country's best-known art.

people.name: Eugenio Espejo
people.why: Indigenous and Black by birth, he became a physician and the intellectual father of Ecuadorian independence.

people.name: Jefferson Pérez
people.why: Won Ecuador's first Olympic gold in 1996 and is a national hero for it.

people.name: Manuela Sáenz
people.why: Bolívar's partner and a fighter in her own right, who saved his life in 1828.

people.name: Juan Montalvo
people.why: His pen was so feared that he claimed it had killed a dictator.

events.title: The French Geodesic Mission
events.what: Scientists came to measure the shape of the earth at the equator — and gave the country its name.

events.title: Battle of Pichincha
events.what: Sucre's victory on the slopes above Quito secured independence from Spain.

events.title: Darwin in the Galápagos
events.what: Five weeks among the islands' finches and tortoises fed directly into On the Origin of Species.

events.title: Rights of nature
events.what: Ecuador became the first country to write the rights of nature into its constitution.

culture.label: Nature
culture.text: The Galápagos sit 900 km offshore and are the reason half the world knows the country's name.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Encebollado, a tuna and cassava soup, is the coastal cure for a hangover. Ceviche here comes with popcorn.

culture.label: Craft
culture.text: The 'Panama' hat is Ecuadorian — woven in Montecristi and Cuenca, and named after where it was sold.

culture.label: Geography
culture.text: Quito sits at 2,850 m; the summit of Chimborazo is the furthest point on the surface from the earth's centre.

culture.label: Otavalo
culture.text: The Otavaleño people run one of the Americas' great textile markets and have kept their dress and language.

talkAbout: The Galápagos, and whether they have been.
Coast versus highlands — the rivalry between Guayaquil and Quito is good-natured and constant.
That the Panama hat is actually theirs.
avoid: Ecuador has had a lot of political turbulence and recent problems with organised crime; ask rather than assert. Don't call the hat Panamanian without expecting a correction.

people.name: Evo Morales
people.why: Bolivia's first indigenous president, a former coca growers' union leader, in office 2006–2019.

people.name: Túpac Katari
people.why: Besieged La Paz for six months in an Aymara uprising; his name still stands for indigenous resistance.

people.name: Jaime Escalante
people.why: The Bolivian maths teacher whose Los Angeles classroom became the film Stand and Deliver.

people.name: Adela Zamudio
people.why: Bolivia's first feminist writer; her birthday is the national Day of Women.

people.name: Marina Núñez del Prado
people.why: Carved Andean women out of native stone and wood, and is Bolivia's best-known artist abroad.

events.title: Silver at Potosí
events.what: The Cerro Rico became the richest silver mine on earth and bankrolled the Spanish empire, at an enormous human cost.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Named after Bolívar, with Sucre as its first president.

events.title: Losing the sea
events.what: The War of the Pacific cost Bolivia its coastline; the navy still exists and Sea Day is marked every March.

events.title: The Water War
events.what: Cochabamba forced the reversal of a water privatisation, an early landmark in global anti-privatisation politics.

culture.label: Landscape
culture.text: The Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat on earth and turns into a mirror in the rainy season.

culture.label: Festival
culture.text: Oruro's Carnaval is a UNESCO-listed diablada — thousands of dancers in devil masks, over three days.

culture.label: Dress
culture.text: The cholita's bowler hat and layered skirts are everyday clothing and a statement of Aymara identity.

culture.label: Coca
culture.text: Coca leaf is chewed and brewed for altitude and is legal and ordinary here — quite separate from cocaine.

culture.label: Language
culture.text: Thirty-six languages are official; Quechua and Aymara are spoken by millions.

talkAbout: Altitude, and how to handle it — everyone has advice.
The salt flats, and the best time of year to see them.
Food: salteñas are a morning institution worth asking about.
avoid: Don't conflate coca with cocaine — it's a sore point. The loss of the coastline to Chile is a real national grievance, not a curiosity.

people.name: José Artigas
people.why: Led the fight for independence and for a federal, land-reforming republic; every town has his statue.

people.name: José Mujica
people.why: A former guerrilla who gave away most of his salary and drove a 1987 Beetle while in office.

people.name: Luis Suárez
people.why: Uruguay's record scorer, and the country's most argued-about sporting figure.

people.name: Eduardo Galeano
people.why: Open Veins of Latin America became the continent's most-read political book.

people.name: Juana de Ibarbourou
people.why: Called 'Juana of America' in her own lifetime, and read across the continent.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Britain brokered a settlement creating a buffer state between Argentina and Brazil.

events.title: The first World Cup
events.what: Uruguay hosted and won the first football World Cup, in a stadium built for it in six months.

events.title: The Maracanazo
events.what: Beating Brazil in front of 200,000 people in Rio — probably the most famous upset in football history.

events.title: First to legalise cannabis
events.what: Uruguay became the first country in the world to regulate the whole cannabis market by law.

culture.label: Mate
culture.text: Uruguayans carry a thermos under one arm all day. Consumption per head is the highest anywhere.

culture.label: Candombe
culture.text: Drumming brought by enslaved Africans, still played through Montevideo's streets on Sunday evenings.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Two World Cups and two Olympic golds from a country of three and a half million.

culture.label: Politics
culture.text: Secular since 1917 — Christmas is officially Family Day and Holy Week is Tourism Week.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: The chivito is a steak sandwich of alarming ambition, and asado is taken as seriously as in Argentina.

talkAbout: Mate: how they take it, and the etiquette of the shared gourd.
Football, and 1950 in particular.
How a country this small keeps ending up ahead on social policy.
avoid: Don't treat Uruguay as a smaller Argentina — the comparison gets old fast. Tango, mate and dulce de leche all have contested origins.

people.name: Augusto Roa Bastos
people.why: I, the Supreme is one of the great Latin American dictator novels; he wrote most of it in exile.

people.name: José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia
people.why: Sealed Paraguay off from the world for a quarter-century and built a self-sufficient state.

people.name: Josefina Plá
people.why: Shaped modern Paraguayan letters and ceramics across seventy years of work.

people.name: Agustín Barrios
people.why: One of the greatest classical guitar composers, and the first to record on the instrument.

people.name: José Luis Chilavert
people.why: A goalkeeper who took free kicks and scored 67 goals — an international curiosity and a national favourite.

events.title: The Jesuit reductions
events.what: Mission towns where Guaraní people kept their language and built an economy, until Spain expelled the Jesuits.

events.title: The War of the Triple Alliance
events.what: Paraguay fought Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay at once and lost perhaps 60% of its population — proportionally the deadliest war in modern history.

events.title: The Stroessner dictatorship
events.what: Thirty-five years of one-party rule, the longest in twentieth-century South America.

events.title: Itaipú dam completed
events.what: For decades the largest hydroelectric plant on earth; Paraguay still generates far more power than it uses.

culture.label: Language
culture.text: Guaraní is spoken by most of the population and is co-official — unique in the Americas for an indigenous language.

culture.label: Tereré
culture.text: Mate served ice-cold with herbs, drunk all day in the heat and shared from one gourd.

culture.label: Craft
culture.text: Ñandutí lace, named after a spider's web, is woven in radiating circles in Itauguá.

culture.label: Music
culture.text: The Paraguayan harp is the national instrument, played with a lightness nothing else quite matches.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Sopa paraguaya is not a soup — it's a dense corn and cheese bread, and the confusion is the point of the joke.

talkAbout: Guaraní — ask them to teach you a phrase; they will be pleased you asked.
Tereré, and the herbs they add to it.
The harp, and the music that goes with it.
avoid: The Triple Alliance war is a national trauma, not a piece of trivia. The Stroessner years still divide opinion.

people.name: Cheddi Jagan
people.why: Dentist turned independence leader, and a central figure in Cold War politics in the Caribbean.

people.name: Walter Rodney
people.why: How Europe Underdeveloped Africa reshaped the study of colonialism; he was assassinated at 38.

people.name: Clive Lloyd
people.why: Captained the West Indies through their era of total dominance, winning the first two World Cups.

people.name: Wilson Harris
people.why: A land surveyor in the interior before becoming one of the Caribbean's most demanding writers.

people.name: Aubrey Williams
people.why: Fused Warrau imagery with modernist abstraction and helped found the Caribbean Artists Movement.

events.title: The Berbice slave uprising
events.what: Enslaved people held the colony for almost a year; its leader Cuffy is now a national hero.

events.title: Indentured labour begins
events.what: After abolition, planters brought in workers from India — which is why Guyana is roughly 40% Indo-Guyanese today.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Guyana left British rule as the only English-speaking country in South America.

events.title: Oil offshore
events.what: An enormous find off the coast has made Guyana one of the fastest-growing economies on earth.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Cricket, not football — Guyana plays as part of the West Indies team.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Curry, roti and pepperpot side by side: Indian, African, Portuguese, Chinese and Indigenous cooking in one kitchen.

culture.label: Kaieteur
culture.text: A single drop of 226 m in untouched rainforest, five times the height of Niagara and almost never crowded.

culture.label: Language
culture.text: English is official; Guyanese Creole is what people actually speak, and nine Amerindian languages survive.

culture.label: Orientation
culture.text: Geographically South American, culturally Caribbean — it belongs to CARICOM, not Mercosur.

talkAbout: Cricket, and the West Indies sides of the 1970s and 80s.
Food, and how the Indian and African traditions meet on one plate.
Kaieteur Falls, and the interior most visitors never see.
avoid: Politics splits along Indo- and Afro-Guyanese lines and is genuinely tense. The border dispute with Venezuela over the Essequibo is serious, not academic.

people.name: Anton de Kom
people.why: His book We Slaves of Suriname told the colony's history from the enslaved side; he died in a Nazi camp.

people.name: Clarence Seedorf
people.why: Suriname-born, the only player to win the Champions League with three different clubs.

people.name: Boni
people.why: Led escaped enslaved people in a guerrilla war against the Dutch; the Aluku Maroons carry his name.

people.name: Maria Sibylla Merian
people.why: Sailed to Suriname at 52 to study insects and produced one of the great works of scientific illustration.

people.name: Ruth Wijdenbosch
people.why: A long-serving parliamentarian and a leading voice for women's rights in Surinamese public life.

events.title: Traded for New York
events.what: The Dutch took Suriname from England and gave up New Amsterdam — now Manhattan — in exchange.

events.title: The Maroon treaties
events.what: The Dutch were forced to recognise the independence of escaped-slave communities in the interior, a century before abolition.

events.title: Abolition
events.what: Slavery ended, followed by indentured workers from India and Java — the origin of today's mix.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Suriname left the Netherlands, and about a third of the population moved to the Dutch mainland.

culture.label: Coexistence
culture.text: A mosque and a synagogue stand side by side in Paramaribo and share a car park.

culture.label: Language
culture.text: Dutch is official, but Sranan Tongo is the street lingua franca, alongside Sarnami, Javanese and Maroon languages.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Javanese saoto soup, Indian roti and Creole pom on the same street, often in the same meal.

culture.label: Forest
culture.text: More than 90% forest cover — proportionally the most forested country on earth.

culture.label: Music
culture.text: Kaseko blends Maroon drumming with brass and jazz, and is what a Surinamese party sounds like.

talkAbout: How so many communities live together in a country of barely 600,000.
Food — every group has a dish and they will want you to try all of them.
The interior, the Maroon villages and the rainforest.
avoid: The 1982 December murders and the Bouterse years remain unresolved and painful. Ethnic politics is a delicate subject.
